Among these is His, glory be to Him, oath by "By the sky and the Ṭāriq" (al-ṭāriq, the night-visitor).

He explained it as "the piercing star" (al-najm al-thāqib), whose light pierces. The intended meaning is the genus, not a specific star. Those who specified it as the Pleiades (al-Thurayyā) or Saturn (Zuḥal) — if they meant it as an example, it is correct; if they meant it as a restriction, there is no evidence for it.

The point is that He swore by the sky and its shining stars, each of which is one of His signs indicating His oneness. He named the star "ṭāriq" because it appears at night after being hidden by the light of the sun, so it is likened to the visitor who comes to people or their household at night.

al-Farrāʾ said: "Whatever comes to you at night is a ṭāriq."

al-Zajjāj and al-Mubarrad said: "The ṭāriq is not at daytime." For this reason the Arabs frequently use ṭurūq (visiting) in describing the phantom (al-khayāl), as Dhū al-Rumma said:

"Has Mayy not visited me at times, remembering her, while the hands of the Pleiades were bent toward the western horizons?"

And Jarīr said:

"The seeker of hearts visited you, and this was not the time of visiting, so return in peace."

For this reason it was said: the first to turn away the phantom (al-ṭayf) was Jarīr, and people continued to accept it and honor it like a guest. The phantom and the guest are both not turned away. Another poet said:

"Has Zaynab not visited me at the end of the night? Peace be upon you — is there a request for what has passed?"

The thing sworn to here is the state of the human soul and the attention given to it, and the establishment of guardians over it, and that it is not left neglected; rather, watchers have been assigned over it who record its deeds and count them. So He swore, glory be to Him, that there is no soul but that over it is a guardian from the angels who preserves its deed and its words and counts what it earns of good or evil.

The readers differed over *lammā*: some read it with shadda (emphatic) and some without. Whoever reads it with shadda makes it in the sense of *illā* (except). *Lammā* comes in the sense of *illā* in two places: one after *in* (*in*) as a lightened or heavy particle, as in this place, or as in His saying ﴿And indeed, all of them your Lord will surely pay in full for their deeds﴾; and the second in the case of oaths, like "I ask you by God, *lammā* you did (it)."

Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: whoever reads it lightened, in his view it is the lightened form of the heavy (*al-thaqīla*), and the *lām* in its predicate is the distinguishing *lām* between the negative *in* and the light *in*, and *mā* is superfluous, and *in* is the one with which the oath is introduced, just as it is introduced with the heavy form.

Whoever reads it with shadda, in his view *in* is negative in the sense of *mā*, and *lammā* is in the sense of *illā*. Sībawayh said, quoting al-Khalīl, regarding their saying "I implore you by God, *lammā* you did (it)": the meaning is "except you did (it)."

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 86, verses 5–8 (part 1 of 4):

Al-dafiq (the gushing one) remains in its original form: it is not an active participle used in the sense of a passive one, as some people suppose. Rather, it is like flowing water, standing water, or still water.

There is no disagreement that the intended meaning of al-sulb (the loins) is the loins of the man.

Opinions differ regarding al-taraʼib (the breastbones/ribs area). It has been said that what is meant by them is also the man's taraʼib, which are the bones of the chest between the collarbone (al-taraqwah) and the nipple (al-thandwah).

It has also been said that what is meant is the taraʼib of the woman. The first view is more evident, because He, glorified is He, said: ﴿It comes out from between the loins and the taraʼib.﴾

He did not say "it comes out from the loins and the taraʼib." Therefore the man's water must be emerging from between these two different places, just as He said about milk: ﴿from between excrement and blood﴾ [al-Nahl: 66].

Also, He, glorified is He, informed that He created him from a nutfah (drop) in more than one place, and the nutfah is the man's water, as the lexicographers said.

Al-Jawhari said: "The nutfah is clear water, whether little or much, and the nutfah is the man's water; its plural is nutaf."

Also, what is described as gushing and spurting is only the man's water. It is not said that the woman "spurted" the water or "gushed" it. What led the proponents of the other view to hold that was that they saw the lexicographers saying: "The taraʼib is the place of the necklace on the chest."

Al-Zajjaj said: "The lexicographers are unanimous on this," and they recited the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"Slender, fair, not overlapping, its taraʼib polished like a mirror."

This does not indicate that taraʼib is specific to women; rather, it applies to both men and women.

Al-Jawhari said: "Al-taraʼib are the bones of the chest between the collarbone and the nipple."

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is able to return him﴾ [al-Tariq: 8], the correct view is that the pronoun refers to the human being, meaning that Allah is able to restore him on the Day of Resurrection, which is the day on which the secrets are tested. Whoever says "the pronoun refers to the water, meaning that Allah is able to return it into the urethra or into the chest, or to hold it back from emerging," has gone far astray, even though Allah, glorified is He, is capable of that. But the context rejects it, and the Qur'anic method is to argue from the origin and the first creation toward the return and the resurrection. Also, He restricted it with the time clause, which is ﴿the day the secrets are tested﴾ [al-Tariq: 9]. The intent is that He, glorified is He, called upon the human being to contemplate the origin of his creation and his provision, for that clearly indicates to him his return to his Lord.

Shaykh Ibn al-Qayyim also said in (Tuhfat al-Mawdud):

Al-Zajjaj said: "All the lexicographers say: al-taribah is the place of the necklace on the chest, and its plural is taraʼib."

Abu ʻUbaydah said: "Al-taraʼib is the hanging place of the throat on the chest, and this is the view of all the lexicographers." ʻAtaʼ related from Ibn ʻAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it means the loins of the man and the taraʼib of the woman, which is the place of her necklace. This is also the view of al-Kalbi, Muqatil, Sufyan, and the majority of the exegetes, and it agrees with these hadiths. Allah has established this custom in bringing into existence what He brings into being from two origins, such as animals, plants, and other creatures.

Animals come into being from the water of the male and the water of the female, just as plants come into being from water, earth, and air.

For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth; how could He have a son when He has no consort?﴾

For a child cannot be born except from a male and his female partner.

This is not refuted by Adam and Eve, our parents, nor by al-Masih (the Messiah). For Allah, glorified is He, mixed the earth of Adam with water until it became clay, then Allah sent the wind and the sun upon it until it became like pottery, then He breathed the spirit into it; and Hawwa' (Eve) was drawn out from him and was a part of his parts.

As for al-Masih, he was created from the water of Maryam, and the angel breathed. So the breath was for him like a father is for another.

(Refinements and Benefits)

Qays ibn al-Rabiʻ narrated from Sulayman al-Taymi, from Abu ʻUthman al-Nahdi, from ʻUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, who said:

"Indeed, in allusive speech (ma'arid al-kalam) there is what suffices a man from lying."

al-Hakam narrated from Mujahid, from Ibn ʻAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both:

"I would not be pleased with allusive speech in exchange for red camels."

al-Zuhri narrated from Humayd ibn ʻAbd al-Rahman ibn ʻAwf, from his mother Umm Kulthum bint ʻUqbah ibn Abi Muʻayt, who was among the earliest emigrants:

"I did not hear the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) grant a concession in anything that people say is a lie, except in three: a man who reconciles between people, a man who speaks falsely to his wife, and falsehood in war."

The meaning of lying in this is allusive speech, not outright lying.

Mansur said: "They had a way of speaking by which they would ward off punishment and calamities from themselves. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) met a vanguard of the polytheists while he was with a group of his companions, and the polytheists said: 'Who are you?' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'We are from water.' They looked at one another and said: 'The tribes of Yemen are many; perhaps they are of them,' and they left."

By his saying (ﷺ) "We are from water," he intended His saying, exalted is He: ﴿created from gushing water﴾ [al-Tariq: 6].

When ʻAbd Allah ibn Rawahah had intercourse with his slave-girl, his wife saw him. She took a knife and came to him, but found him having completed his need.

She said: "If I had seen you where you were, I would have struck it into your neck."

He said: "What did you do?" She said: "If you are truthful, then recite the Qur'an."

He said:

"I testify that the promise of Allah is true, and that the Fire is the abode of the disbelievers.
And that the Throne floats above the water, and above the Throne is the Lord of the worlds.
And carrying it are strong angels, the angels of God, marked."

She said: "I believed in the Book of Allah and denied my own eyes."

This reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he laughed until his molar teeth showed.

Ibn ʻAbd al-Barr said: "This is established from ʻAbd Allah ibn Rawahah."

It is reported from ʻUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "I am amazed at one who knows allusive speech; how does he lie?"

Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, was invited to a meal and said: "I am fasting." Then they saw him eating. They said: "Did you not say, 'I am fasting'?"

He said: "Did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) not say: 'Fasting three days of every month is like fasting the whole year'?"

Muhammad ibn Sirin, when a creditor demanded payment from him and he had nothing with him, would say: "I will give you on one of the two days, God willing." He would be understood to mean that day and the one after it, but he meant the two days of this world and the Hereafter.

(Section)

When you reflect on what Allah, glorified is He, called His servants to contemplate in His Book, it will lead you to knowledge of Him, glorified and exalted is He, and of His oneness, His attributes of perfection, and the descriptions of His majesty: the all-encompassing scope of His power and knowledge, the perfection of His wisdom, His mercy, His beneficence, His kindness, His gentleness, His justice, His pleasure and His anger, His reward and His punishment. Through this He made Himself known to His servants and urged them to reflect upon His signs. We will mention some examples of what Allah, glorified is He, mentioned in His Book, by which one may infer others. Among them is the creation of man, about which He, glorified is He, urged reflection and contemplation in more than one place in His Book, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So let man look at what he was created from.﴾

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And within yourselves; will you not see?﴾

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, indeed We created you from dust, then from a drop, then from a clinging clot, then from a lump of flesh, formed and unformed, that We may make clear to you. And We settle in the wombs whatever We will for a specified term, then We bring you out as a child, then that you may reach your maturity. And among you is one who is taken in death, and among you is one who is returned to the most abject age, so that he knows nothing after having known.﴾

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Does man think he will be left neglected? Was he not a drop of semen emitted? Then he became a clinging clot, and He created and proportioned him, and made of him two mates, the male and the female. Is not He able to bring the dead to life?﴾

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Did We not create you from a worthless fluid, then place it in a secure place for a known term? Then We determined, and how excellent are We as determiners.﴾

And He said: ﴿Does man not see that We created him from a drop, and then he is a clear adversary?﴾

And He said: ﴿And We certainly created man from an extract of clay. Then We placed him as a drop in a secure place. Then We made the drop a clinging clot, then We made the clot a lump, then We made the lump bones, then We clothed the bones with flesh; then We produced him as another creation. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators.﴾

This is frequent in the Qur'an, calling the servant to look and reflect upon the beginning of his creation, its middle, and its end. For his own self and his creation are among the greatest proofs of his Creator and Originator, and nothing is closer to man than himself. In it are wonders that indicate the greatness of Allah, such that lifetimes pass without grasping part of them, while he is heedless of them and turns away from reflecting on them. Had he reflected upon his own self, what he would know of the wonders of its creation would have restrained him from his disbelief. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Woe to man, how ungrateful he is! From what thing did He create him? From a drop He created him and determined him. Then He made the way easy for him. Then He causes him to die and buries him. Then, when He wills, He will raise him up again.﴾

Therefore, the Exalted has not repeated for our ears and minds the mention of this, so that we would hear the words *nutfah* (a drop of semen), *ʿalaqah* (a clinging clot), *mudghah* (a lump of flesh), and *turab* (dust), nor merely to utter them, nor merely to inform us of that. Rather, it is for a matter beyond all of this, which is the purpose of the address, and to which this discourse leads. So consider now the *nutfah* with the eye of insight. It is a drop of despised, weak, filthy water. If an hour passed over it, it would rot and stink. How did the Lord of lords, the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, extract it from between the backbone and the ribs, submissive to His power, obedient to His will, made docile in its movement despite the narrowness of its paths and the variety of its channels, until He drove it to its place of rest and gathering? And how did the Exalted join the male and the female, cast love between them, and by the chain of desire and affection lead them to the union that is the cause of the child's formation and creation? And how did He determine the joining of those two waters, though each is far from the other, driving them from the depths of the veins and organs and gathering them in one place, and giving them a firm settlement that no air can reach to corrupt it, nor cold by His praise, nor any accident that could reach it, nor any blight that could overpower it?

Then He turned that white drop, mixed with color, into a red clot inclining to blackness. Then He made it a lump of flesh, differing from the clot in its color, its reality and its form. Then He made it bones, bare, with no covering upon them, differing from the lump in shape, form, measure, texture and color. And consider how He divided those similar and equal parts into nerves, bones, veins, tendons, the dry and the soft, and what lies between them. Then how He bound some of them to others with the strongest and firmest bond, furthest from dissolution. And how He covered them with flesh, which He set upon them, making it a container, a covering and a guardian for them, and making them bearers of it and sustainers of it, so that the flesh subsists by them and they are preserved by it. And how He shaped them, giving them the best form, and split for them hearing, sight, mouth, nose and all the other openings, extended the two hands and the two feet and spread them out, and divided their extremities with fingers, then divided the fingers into joints. He assembled the inner organs: the heart, the stomach, the liver, the spleen, the lungs, the womb, the bladder and the intestines, each of which has a measure specific to it and a benefit specific to it.

Then consider the perfect wisdom in the structure of the bones as the support and pillar of the body. And how their Lord and Creator determined them with varying measures and varying shapes: some small, some large, some long, some short, some curved, some round, some thin, some broad, some solid, and some hollow. And how He assembled some within others: some whose assembly is like the male within the female, and some whose assembly is only a joining. And how their shapes vary according to the variation of their benefits, like the molars, for since they are the instrument of grinding, they were made broad; and since the teeth are the instrument of cutting, they were made pointed and sharp. And since the human being needs movement with the whole body and with some of its limbs, to move about for his needs, He did not make his bones one bone, but many bones, and placed between them joints so that movement might be easy through them, and the measure and shape of each one were set according to the movement required of it. And how He tightened the joints and limbs and bound some to others with tendons and ligaments, which He grew from one end of the bone and attached one end of the bone to the other end like a band for it. Then He placed on one end of the bone projections extending outward from it, and on the other end hollows sunk into it, matching the shape of those projections, so that they enter into them and fit upon them. So when the servant wishes to move a part of his body, it is not hindered for him. And had there been no joints, that movement would have been impossible for him.

And reflect on the manner of the creation of the head and the great number of bones in it, to the point that it is said they are fifty-five bones of differing shapes, measures and benefits. And how the Exalted set it upon the body and made it high, like the height of a rider over his mount. And since it is high above the body, He placed in it the five senses and all the instruments of perception: hearing, sight, smell, taste and touch. And He placed the organ of sight at its front, so that it would be like a vanguard, a sentinel and a scout for the body. And He constructed each eye of seven layers, each layer having a specific description, a specific measure and a specific benefit, such that if one of those seven layers were lost or moved from its form and place, the eye would be disabled from seeing. Then the Exalted set, within those seven layers, a wondrous creation, which is the pupil of the eye, the size of the lens, by which it sees what is between the east and the west, and the earth and the sky. He made it in the eye as the heart is among the organs: it is its king, and those layers, the eyelids and the lashes are its servants, its screen and its guards. "So blessed be Allah, the best of creators" (23:14).

Consider how the form, shape and measure of the two eyes are beautiful, then how He made the eyelids a covering, a shield, a protection and an adornment for them. Thus they receive from the eye harm, dust and grime, and shield it from the harmful cold and the harmful heat. Then He planted on the edges of those eyelids the lashes, as beauty and adornment, and for other benefits beyond beauty and adornment. Then He deposited in them that seeing light and dazzling radiance which pierces what is between the sky and the earth, and then pierces the sky, reaching beyond the sight of what lies above it, of the stars. The Exalted has deposited this wondrous secret in this small measure, such that the image of the heavens is impressed in it despite the vastness of their expanses and the remoteness of their horizons.

He split for it hearing, and created the ear in the best of its creation and most effective in achieving its purpose. He made it hollow like a seashell, to gather the sound and convey it to the ear canal, and so that it may sense the crawling of an insect within it, and hasten to remove it. He placed in it folds, hollows and windings that hold the entering air and sound, breaking their sharpness, and then conveying them to the ear canal. And one of the wisdoms in this is that the path becomes long for the creature, so it does not reach the ear canal until it awakens or is alerted by its holding. There is also in it other wisdom beside this.

Then the wisdom of the Lord, the Creator, the Exalted, required that He make the water of the ear extremely bitter, so that no creature passes it or cuts through it entering the inner ear; rather, when it reaches it, the ear devises the means for its return. And He made the water of the eyes salty, to preserve them, for they are a delicate fat susceptible to corruption, so the saltiness of their water is for their protection and preservation. And He made the water of the mouth sweet and pleasant, so that by it one perceives the tastes of things as they are. For if it were otherwise, it would transform them to its own nature, just as whoever has bitterness in his mouth finds the tastes of things that are not bitter to be bitter, as it is said:

"And whoever has a bitter mouth, being sick,
finds the pure water bitter to him."

And He, glorified is He, set the bridge of the nose upon the face, so He beautified its form, shape and placement. He opened in it two nostrils and separated them with a partition. He deposited in them the sense of smell (ḥāssat al-shamm) by which one perceives the various kinds of scents, the pleasant and the foul, the beneficial and the harmful, so that one may draw air through it and it may carry the air to the heart, which is refreshed and nourished by it. Then He did not place within it the twists and folds that He placed in the ear, lest it retain the scent, weaken it and cut off its passage. He made it an outlet into which the superfluities of the brain descend and gather, and from which they then exit. His wisdom required that its upper part be narrower than its lower part, because if its lower part were wide, those superfluities would gather in it and exit with ease. Also, it takes in air, fills itself, and then rises a little along its passage until it reaches the heart, arriving without harming or disturbing it. Then He separated the two nostrils with a partition between them, as a wisdom and a mercy from Him. For since it is a conduit and a passage that shields what descends from the head and the breath that rises through it, He placed in its middle a partition so that it would not be corrupted by what flows through it, and so that it would not prevent the inhaling of breath. Rather, either the superfluities descending from one of the two openings generally settle there, leaving the other for breathing, or they flow through both and divide, so the nose is never fully blocked and there remains an entrance for breathing. Furthermore, since it is one organ and one sense, and not two organs and two senses like the two ears and the two eyes, whose plurality wisdom required, it may happen that one of them is afflicted or exposed to a calamity that prevents it from perfect function, while the other remains sound, so the benefit of this sense is not entirely lost. Since the presence of two noses on the face would be a conspicuous thing, He set one nose upon it and placed in it two openings, separated by a partition, which operates in the manner of the plurality of the two eyes and ears in benefit, though it is one. So blessed is Allah, the Lord of the worlds, the best of creators.

He, glorified is He, split the mouth for the servant in the best place and fitted it for him, and deposited in it benefits and the instruments of taste and speech, and the instruments of grinding and cutting, whose wonders dazzle the intellects. He deposited in it the tongue, which is one of His signs that point to Him, and He made it the interpreter of the king of the organs, clarifying and conveying on his behalf. Just as He made the ear a messenger who conveys and delivers to him, so it is his courier that conveys information to him, while the tongue is his courier and messenger who conveys on his behalf what he wants. His wisdom, glorified is He, required that this messenger be protected, guarded and concealed, not exposed or uncovered, like the ear, the eye and the nose. For those organs, since they convey from the outside to him, were made prominent and apparent. But since the tongue conveys from him to the outside, He made for it a protected covering, because there is no benefit in exposing it, since it does not take anything from the outside to the heart. Also, since it is the most noble of the organs after the heart, and its position relative to the heart is that of its interpreter and vizier, He spread over it a canopy that veils and protects it, and placed within that canopy like the heart within the chest. Furthermore, it is among the most delicate and soft of the organs, and the most moist, and it acts only through the moisture surrounding it. Had it been exposed, it would be subject to heat, dryness and desiccation, which would prevent it from acting, along with other wisdoms and benefits.

Then He, glorified is He, adorned the mouth with the teeth it contains, which are its beauty and adornment, and by which the servant's sustenance and nourishment are sustained. He made some of them grinders for crushing and some tools for cutting. He made their roots firm, sharpened their tips, whitened their color, and arranged their rows with equal tips and harmonious order, as if they were pearls strung together in whiteness, clarity and beauty. Glorified is He, He encircled this with two walls and deposited in them benefits and wisdoms, namely the two lips. He made their color, shape, placement and form beautiful, and made them a covering and lid for the mouth. He made them the completion of the articulation points of speech and its final limit, just as He made the farthest part of the throat its beginning, and the tongue and what is adjacent to it its middle. For this reason most of the work of articulation is done by them, since they are the intermediary. His wisdom required that He make the lips pure flesh, without bone or sinew, so that by them one may be able to suck drinks, and so that their opening and closing would be easy for him. He singled out the lower jaw for movement, because moving the lighter part is better, and because it contains the noble organs, so He did not risk them in motion.

Glorified is He, He created the throats of different shapes, in narrowness and breadth, roughness and smoothness, hardness and softness, length and shortness. Thus voices differ enormously, and two voices hardly resemble one another except rarely. For this reason the sound opinion is that the testimony of a blind man is accepted, since he distinguishes between persons by their voices just as the seeing person distinguishes them by their appearances, and the confusion that occurs between voices is like the confusion that occurs between forms.

Glorified is He, He adorned the head with hair and made it a garment for it, because it needs it. He adorned the face with the various shapes and measures of hair that He grew upon it. He adorned it with the eyebrows, made them a shield against what drips from the scalp to the eyes, shaped their arch and beautified their line. He adorned the eyelids with eyelashes. He also adorned the face with the beard, and made it a perfection, dignity and majesty for a man. He adorned the lips with what He grew above them as the mustache and below them as the goatee. Likewise, glorified is He, He created the two hands, which are the servant's instrument, his weapon and the capital of his livelihood. He made their length such that they reach whatever part of his body he wishes, and He made the palm broad so that he may grasp and open. He divided it into five fingers, divided each finger into three phalanges, and the thumb into two. He placed the four fingers on one side and the thumb on the other, so that the thumb can turn to all of them. Thus they came in the best arrangement, suited for grasping, spreading, and handling tasks. Even if the first and the last of mankind were to gather to devise, by the subtlety of their thinking, another arrangement of the fingers besides this one, they would find no way to it. Blessed is He who, had He willed, would have made them otherwise. Had He made them one flat sheet like a plate, the servant could not have accomplished his interests, the various kinds of his dealings, the delicate crafts, writing, and other things. If he spread his fingers they would be a tray upon which he places what he wishes; if he gathered and clenched them they would be a club and an instrument for striking; and if he placed them between closing and spreading they would be a ladle with which he takes and holds what he grasps. He set the nails upon their tips as an adornment, support and protection, and so that he may pick up with them fine things that the finger-flesh cannot reach. He made them a weapon against other animals and birds, an instrument for his livelihood, and so that a person may scratch his body with them when needed. Thus the nail, which is the least and most insignificant of things, if a person lacked it and then an itch appeared, his need for it would become intense, and nothing could take its place in scratching his body. Then He guided the hand to the place of the itch so that it reaches it, even in sleep and heedlessness, without any need to seek. Had he asked someone else, he would not have found the place of the itch except after fatigue and hardship.

Then consider the profound wisdom in making the bones of the lower body thick and strong, because they are its foundation, while the bones of its upper part are less thick and hard, because they are carried. Then consider how He made the neck a support for the head. He composed it of seven hollow, round vertebrae, placed some upon others, and fitted each vertebra with a firm and precise joint, until they became as if they were one vertebra. Then He set the neck upon the back and the chest. Then He composed the back from its top to the end of the sacrum of twenty-four vertebrae, set one within another, which are the junction of his ribs and which hold them so that they do not come loose and separate. Then He connected these bones to one another: the bones of the back to the bones of the chest, the bones of the shoulders to the bones of the upper arms, the upper arms to the forearms, and the forearms to the palm and fingers. Consider how He clothed the broad bones, like those of the back and head, with a covering of flesh suited to them, and the fine bones with a covering suited to them, like the fingers, and the medium bones likewise, like the bones of the forearms and upper arms. Thus the body is composed of three hundred and sixty bones and two hundred and forty-eight joints, and the rest are small bones filling the spaces between the joints. Had it gained one bone, it would have been a harm to the person requiring its removal. Had it lost one bone, it would have been a deficiency requiring its setting. The physician looks at these bones and the manner of their composition to know how to set them, and the knowing one looks at them to infer the greatness of their Maker, Creator, His wisdom, His knowledge and His subtlety. How great is the difference between the two views!

Then, glorified is He, He tied those organs and parts with ligaments, binding their joints and holding them like pegs that secure and preserve them, until their number reached five hundred and twenty-nine ligaments. They differ in thickness, thinness, length, shortness, straightness and bending according to the differences of their places and positions. Of them He made twenty-four ligaments as instruments for moving the eye, opening and closing it, and seeing with it. Should one of these ligaments be cut, the matter of the eye would be disturbed. Likewise, each organ has ligaments that belong to it, like the instruments by which it moves, acts and does everything. All of this is the work of the Wise Lord and the decree of the Mighty, the Knowing, in a drop of contemptible water. So woe to the deniers, and remoteness to the deniers. (Among the wonders of His creation is that He made in the head three chambers, one passing into another: a chamber at the front, a chamber in the middle, and a chamber at the back. He deposited in those chambers some of His secrets, including memory, thought and understanding.)

Among the wonders of His creation are the inner matters that are not seen, such as the heart, the liver, the spleen, the lungs, the intestines, the bladder, and all the other wondrous instruments within the belly, with their various and diverse benefits. As for the heart, it is the king who uses all the instruments of the body and employs them. It is surrounded by them, served and attended, located in the middle. It is the most noble of the organs of the body, by it subsists life, and it is the source of the animal spirit (al-rūḥ al-ḥayawānī) and the innate heat (al-ḥarāra al-gharīziyya). It is the mine of intellect, knowledge, forbearance, courage, generosity, patience, tolerance, love, will, contentment, anger, and all the other attributes of perfection. All the outer and inner organs and their powers are only soldiers of the heart's army. The eye is its scout and forerunner, which uncovers for it what is seen. When it sees something, it conveys it to the heart, and because of the strong connection between them, when something settles in the heart, it appears in the eyes. They are its mirror, translating for the beholder what is within it, just as the tongue is its interpreter, conveying to the hearing what is in it. For this reason Allah, glorified is He, often mentions these three together in His Book, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart, all of those will be questioned about.﴾ And His saying: ﴿And We made for them hearing and sight and hearts.﴾ And His saying: ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind.﴾ This has already been mentioned. Likewise He pairs the heart and sight, as in His saying: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sights.﴾ And His saying concerning His Messenger Muhammad: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw.﴾ Then He said: ﴿His sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress.﴾

Likewise the ear is its messenger who conveys to it, and the tongue is its interpreter. In sum, all the other organs are its servants and soldiers. The Prophet said: "Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Verily, it is the heart." Abu Hurayrah said: "The heart is a king and the organs are its soldiers. If the king is good, his soldiers are good, and if the king is corrupt, his soldiers are corrupt." The lungs were made for it like a fan that cools it constantly, because it is the most heated of the organs; indeed, it is the source of heat itself.

As for the brain, which is the marrow, it was made cold, and there has been disagreement about the wisdom of this. One group said that the brain was made cold to cool the heat of the heart and bring it from excess to moderation. Another group rejected this and said: If that were so, the brain would not be far from the heart; rather, it should surround it like the lungs, or be close to it in the chest, to break its heat. The first group replied that the brain's distance from the heart does not negate the wisdom we have mentioned, for if it were close, the heat of the heart would overpower it with its strength. So the distance between them was set such that neither corrupts the other, and the temperament of each is balanced by the temperament of the other. This is unlike the lungs, which are an instrument for cooling the heart and were not made to moderate its heat. A third group took a middle position and said: Rather, the marrow is hot but of lukewarm heat, and it has coolness by its nature, for it is the source of the mind. For this reason the mind needs a place that is still, steady, clear of filth and turbidity, free from clamor and noise. Therefore the excellence of thought, recollection, and drawing out the correct view occurs when the body is at rest, its movements are slack, and its preoccupations and disturbances are few. For this reason the heart was not suitable for these functions, while the brain was moderate in this and suited to them. Thus these acts flourish at night and in empty places, and they are corrupted when the fire of anger and desire flares, when there is intense worry, and with fatigue and strong bodily and psychological movements. This discussion is linked to another principle: whether the senses and the intellect have their origin in the heart or in the brain. One group said that all of them originate in the heart, and the senses are connected to it, with channels and passages between it and the senses. They said: each of these organs that are the instruments of the senses has a connection with the heart by nerves and other means, and these nerves come out from the heart until they reach each of these bodies in which the senses are. They said: when the eye sees something, it conveys it through the instrument within it to the heart, because that instrument is connected from it to the heart. When the hearing perceives a sound, it conveys it to the heart, and likewise every sense. Then they raised a question for themselves, saying: If it is asked, how can one organ be of various mixtures, sustained by many different senses, while the bodies of these senses are different, and the power of each sense differs from the power of the other sense? They answered that all the veins in the body are connected to the heart, either directly or through an intermediary. There is no vein or organ that does not have a connection with the heart, close or distant. They said: From it, through those veins and channels, there issues to each organ what is suitable and similar to it. So from it issues to the two eyes what produces the sense of sight, to the two ears what they perceive of sounds, to the flesh what produces the sense of touch, to the nose what produces the sense of smell, to the tongue what produces the sense of taste, and to every possessor of a power what supplies and preserves its power. It is thus the supplier of these organs, senses and powers. For this reason the sound opinion is that it is the first of the organs to come into being. They said: there is no doubt that the origin of the rational faculty (al-quwwa al-ʿāqila) is from it, though others disagreed on this and said: Rather, the intellect is in the head. The correct view is that its origin and source are in the heart, while its branches and fruit are in the head. The Qur'an indicates this in His saying: ﴿Have they not traveled through the land, so that they have hearts with which to understand?﴾ And He said: ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart.﴾

I have translated the passage as given. Please note that the text includes a few lines where the Arabic is not fully clear, which I have rendered as closely as possible.

The heart mentioned here is not the lump of flesh shared by animals. What is meant is what it contains of intellect and understanding. Another group disputed this and said the source of these senses is only the brain. They denied that there are nerves or vessels between the heart and the eye, the ear and the nose, and said this is a false claim about the creation. The correct position is a middle ground between the two groups: a power emanates from the heart to these senses, and it is a spiritual power that does not need specific channels and nerves carrying it in order to reach them. The arrival of powers to these senses and organs depends only on their receptivity and readiness, and the heart's supply does not depend on channels and nerves. With this, the confusion in this matter is removed, a matter in which the discussion has grown long and the dispute and contention have multiplied. And God knows best, and to Him belongs success in what is right.

The purpose is to draw attention to the least of the wisdoms in the creation of man, and the matter is many times greater than what comes to mind or can be expressed in speech. The benefit of mentioning this fragment, which is everything in relation to what lies beyond it, is to draw attention. If the servant looks at his food alone, from its entrance, its place of settling and its exit, he sees in it lessons and wonders: how an instrument was made for him to take it with, then a gate through which it enters, then an instrument that cuts it into small pieces, then a grinder that grinds it, then glands with water that kneads it, then a channel and a path beside the windpipe, where this descends and that ascends, so they never meet despite extreme closeness. Then he was given intestines and passages that bring it to the stomach, which is its storehouse and place of gathering. It has two openings: an upper opening through which the food enters, and a lower opening through which its waste exits. The upper opening is wider than the lower, since the upper is the entrance for what is gained and the lower is the outlet for what is harmful from it. The lower opening is always closed so that the food may remain in its place. When digestion is complete, that gate opens until the expulsion is finished, and it is called the gatekeeper for this reason. The upper one is called the mouth of the stomach. The food descends into the stomach in lumps, and when it settles there it melts and dissolves. Around the stomach, both inside and outside, is a fiery heat, perhaps even exceeding the heat of fire, by which the food is cooked within it, just as food is cooked in a pot by the fire surrounding it. For this reason it dissolves what is hardened like pebbles and other things, until it leaves it liquid. When it dissolves, its pure part rises upward and its turbid part sinks downward. From the stomach there are veins connected to the whole body, through which the known requirement of each organ and its substance is sent, according to its readiness and receptivity. It sends what is most noble, subtle and light of this to the spirits: to the sight it sends sight, to the hearing hearing, to the smell smell, and to each sense according to its nature. This is the finest of what is generated from food. Then from it is sent to the brain what suits it in subtlety and balance, then what remains is sent to the organs through those channels according to their nature, and from it is sent to the bones, hair and nails what nourishes and preserves them. Thus the food enters the stomach by ways and channels, and leaves it to the organs by ways and channels. This coming in and this going out is perfect wisdom and abundant blessing.

Since food, when transformed in the stomach, is transformed into blood, black bile, yellow bile and phlegm, His wisdom, glorified and exalted be He, required that each of these humours have an outlet toward which it is directed and in which it gathers, and that none be sent to the noble organs except the most refined. So He placed the gall bladder as the outlet for yellow bile, and placed the spleen as the seat for black bile, and the liver absorbs what is most noble of this, which is blood, and then sends it to the whole body through a single vessel that divides into many channels, delivering to each hair, nerve, bone and vein what sustains its substance. Then when you consider the inner and outer powers within him, differing in themselves and in their benefits, you see wonders of wonders: such as the power of his hearing, sight, smell, taste and touch, his love and hatred, his contentment and anger, and other powers related to perception and will, and likewise the powers that act upon his food, such as the power that cooks it, the power that retains it, the power that pushes it to the organs, and the digestive power after the organs have taken what they need from it, and other wonders of his outward and inward creation.

(Section)

Now return to the drop of sperm and consider its state first and what it became afterward. If mankind and the jinn were to gather to create for it hearing, sight, intellect, power, knowledge or a spirit, or even one of its smallest bones, or even one of its finest veins, or even one single hair, they would be unable to do so. Rather, all of this is a trace of the making of God, who perfected everything in a drop of despised water.

If this is His making in a drop of water, then how is His making in the kingdom of the heavens, their height, their vastness, their roundness, the greatness of their creation, the excellence of their structure, the wonders of their sun, moon and stars, their measures and shapes, and the variation of their risings and settings? Not an atom in them is devoid of wisdom. Rather, they are more perfect in creation, more exact in making, and comprehensive of wonders beyond the human body. Indeed, there is no comparison between everything on earth and the wonders of the heavens. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Are you more difficult to create or is the heaven? He built it, raised its height and made it proportionate.﴾ [79:27–28]

And he said in al-Tibyan.

Then, glorified is He, drew man's attention to the proof of the resurrection through what he witnesses of his own origin, following the Qur'anic method of proving the resurrection through the beginning. He said: ﴿So let man look at what he was created from﴾ [86:5], meaning: let him look with the gaze of reflection and inference, so that he may know that the One who began his first creation from a drop is able to restore him.

Then He informed that He created him from a gushing water. Dafq means pouring water; it is said: "I poured the water, so it is poured (madfuq) and gushing (dafiq) and poured out (mundafiq)." The madfuq is that upon which your action fell, like the broken and the struck. The mutadaffiq is the one affected by the action of the doer; you say "I poured it, so it poured out," as you say "I broke it, so it broke." The dafiq is said to be an active participle with the sense of a passive, like the phrases "a hidden secret" and "a pleasant life." It is also said to be a relative form, not a verbal one, meaning "possessing gushing," and that flowing is not intended as an action. It is also said, and this is correct, that it is an active participle in its proper sense, and it does not follow that it is the doer of the gushing, since the active participle is the one in whom the action subsists, whether he performed it or another did, just as one says "flowing water" and "a dead man," though he did not cause death, but because death subsists in him he is ascribed to it in the manner of action. This is not rejected in the language of any nation, let alone the broadest and most eloquent languages. As for "a pleasant life," describing it that way is better than describing it as "a pleasing one," since it is the fitting one for them; so this is likened to its being pleased with them, as they were pleased with it, as if it were pleased with them and they with it. This is more emphatic than merely calling it pleasing. Reflect on this. And since they say "the present time" and "the current hour," though these do not act, how could it be impossible for them to say "gushing water" and "a pleasant life"?

By describing it as gushing, He drew attention to its weakness and lack of cohesion. Then He mentioned its place from which it exits, which is between the spine and the ribs. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The spine of the man and the ribs of the woman," which is the place of the necklace on her chest. The child is created from both waters together. It is also said: the spine of the man and his ribs, which is his chest, so it exits from his spine and chest. This verse, which indicates the power of the Creator, is like His bringing forth pure milk from between dung and blood.

Then He mentioned the matter inferred and the resurrection by His saying: ﴿Indeed He is able to return him﴾ [86:8], meaning: able to return him to life on the Day of Resurrection, just as He is able to create him from such water. This is the sound meaning of the verse. There are two weak opinions: one is Mujahid's, that it refers to returning the water into the urethra; the other is that of ʿIkrimah and al-Dahhak, that it refers to returning the water into the spine. A third view is that of Muqatil: "If You will, You may return him from old age to youth, from youth to childhood, and to the drop."

The correct view is the first, for several reasons. First, it is the known method of the Qur'an to infer the resurrection from the beginning. Second, this is more conclusive for the intended point than the ability to return water into the urethra. Third, no parallel to this meaning occurs elsewhere in the Qur'an, and no one has denied it so that God would need to establish proof against him. Fourth, He restricted the action with a time expression, His saying: ﴿On the day the secrets are tested﴾ [86:9], which is the Day of Resurrection, meaning that God is able to return him alive on that day. Fifth, the pronoun in "His return" is the pronoun in His saying: ﴿He will have no power nor any helper﴾ [86:10], and this certainly refers to man, not to the water. Sixth, there is no mention of the urethra that would determine the thing to which the return refers; so if someone said "able to return it to the opening into which it was poured," there would be no difference between him and this view, and it would be no better than it. Seventh, returning water into the urethra or the spine after it has left is neither known nor a customary matter in which power has been exercised, though it is within the Lord's power, but He has not done it, and custom has not been applied to it, and it is not something people have spoken about either by denial or affirmation. Such a matter the Lord would not establish or argue for, nor would He warn against its deniers; He argues only for a fact that has occurred or will certainly occur.

If it is said: He, exalted is He, has said: ﴿Does man think that We will not gather his bones? Yes, We are able to restore even his fingertips﴾ [75:3–4], meaning: to make them like a camel's hoof. It is said that this too has two views: one is this, and the second, which is more likely, is that restoring his fingertips means restoring them as they were after decay had scattered them in the dust. Eighth, He, glorified is He, called man to reflect on what he was created from in order to turn him away from denying what He informed him of, and He did not inform him of the power of his Creator to return water into his urethra after it has departed from him, so that He would call him to reflect on what he was created from, in order to make him see as shameful the denial of the possibility of returning the water. Ninth, there is no connection between reflecting on the origin of his creation and returning water into the urethra after it has exited, nor any necessary link between them, so as to make one a proof for the possibility of the other. This differs from the connection between the origin and the resurrection, the first creation and the second, the first growth and the second, which is a connection in many respects, such that the possibility of one entails the possibility of the other and the occurrence of one entails the correctness of the occurrence of the other; hence it is good to infer one from the other. Tenth, He, glorified is He, drew attention by His saying: ﴿There is over every soul a guardian﴾ [86:4] that He has appointed over him one who keeps watch over his deeds and records them, so nothing is lost from him. Then by His saying: ﴿Indeed He is able to return him﴾ He drew attention to His ability to raise him to be recompensed for the deed that was kept and recorded. Thus He mentioned the state of the origin of his deeds and their end: their origin is preserved for him, and their end is the recompense for them. He drew attention to this by His saying: ﴿On the day the secrets are tested﴾.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 86, verses 5–8 (part 1 of 4):

Al-dafiq (the gushing one) remains in its original form: it is not an active participle used in the sense of a passive one, as some people suppose. Rather, it is like flowing water, standing water, or still water.

There is no disagreement that the intended meaning of al-sulb (the loins) is the loins of the man.

Opinions differ regarding al-taraʼib (the breastbones/ribs area). It has been said that what is meant by them is also the man's taraʼib, which are the bones of the chest between the collarbone (al-taraqwah) and the nipple (al-thandwah).

It has also been said that what is meant is the taraʼib of the woman. The first view is more evident, because He, glorified is He, said: ﴿It comes out from between the loins and the taraʼib.﴾

He did not say "it comes out from the loins and the taraʼib." Therefore the man's water must be emerging from between these two different places, just as He said about milk: ﴿from between excrement and blood﴾ [al-Nahl: 66].

Also, He, glorified is He, informed that He created him from a nutfah (drop) in more than one place, and the nutfah is the man's water, as the lexicographers said.

Al-Jawhari said: "The nutfah is clear water, whether little or much, and the nutfah is the man's water; its plural is nutaf."

Also, what is described as gushing and spurting is only the man's water. It is not said that the woman "spurted" the water or "gushed" it. What led the proponents of the other view to hold that was that they saw the lexicographers saying: "The taraʼib is the place of the necklace on the chest."

Al-Zajjaj said: "The lexicographers are unanimous on this," and they recited the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"Slender, fair, not overlapping, its taraʼib polished like a mirror."

This does not indicate that taraʼib is specific to women; rather, it applies to both men and women.

Al-Jawhari said: "Al-taraʼib are the bones of the chest between the collarbone and the nipple."

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is able to return him﴾ [al-Tariq: 8], the correct view is that the pronoun refers to the human being, meaning that Allah is able to restore him on the Day of Resurrection, which is the day on which the secrets are tested. Whoever says "the pronoun refers to the water, meaning that Allah is able to return it into the urethra or into the chest, or to hold it back from emerging," has gone far astray, even though Allah, glorified is He, is capable of that. But the context rejects it, and the Qur'anic method is to argue from the origin and the first creation toward the return and the resurrection. Also, He restricted it with the time clause, which is ﴿the day the secrets are tested﴾ [al-Tariq: 9]. The intent is that He, glorified is He, called upon the human being to contemplate the origin of his creation and his provision, for that clearly indicates to him his return to his Lord.

Shaykh Ibn al-Qayyim also said in (Tuhfat al-Mawdud):

Al-Zajjaj said: "All the lexicographers say: al-taribah is the place of the necklace on the chest, and its plural is taraʼib."

Abu ʻUbaydah said: "Al-taraʼib is the hanging place of the throat on the chest, and this is the view of all the lexicographers." ʻAtaʼ related from Ibn ʻAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it means the loins of the man and the taraʼib of the woman, which is the place of her necklace. This is also the view of al-Kalbi, Muqatil, Sufyan, and the majority of the exegetes, and it agrees with these hadiths. Allah has established this custom in bringing into existence what He brings into being from two origins, such as animals, plants, and other creatures.

Animals come into being from the water of the male and the water of the female, just as plants come into being from water, earth, and air.

For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth; how could He have a son when He has no consort?﴾

For a child cannot be born except from a male and his female partner.

This is not refuted by Adam and Eve, our parents, nor by al-Masih (the Messiah). For Allah, glorified is He, mixed the earth of Adam with water until it became clay, then Allah sent the wind and the sun upon it until it became like pottery, then He breathed the spirit into it; and Hawwa' (Eve) was drawn out from him and was a part of his parts.

As for al-Masih, he was created from the water of Maryam, and the angel breathed. So the breath was for him like a father is for another.

(Refinements and Benefits)

Qays ibn al-Rabiʻ narrated from Sulayman al-Taymi, from Abu ʻUthman al-Nahdi, from ʻUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, who said:

"Indeed, in allusive speech (ma'arid al-kalam) there is what suffices a man from lying."

al-Hakam narrated from Mujahid, from Ibn ʻAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both:

"I would not be pleased with allusive speech in exchange for red camels."

al-Zuhri narrated from Humayd ibn ʻAbd al-Rahman ibn ʻAwf, from his mother Umm Kulthum bint ʻUqbah ibn Abi Muʻayt, who was among the earliest emigrants:

"I did not hear the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) grant a concession in anything that people say is a lie, except in three: a man who reconciles between people, a man who speaks falsely to his wife, and falsehood in war."

The meaning of lying in this is allusive speech, not outright lying.

Mansur said: "They had a way of speaking by which they would ward off punishment and calamities from themselves. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) met a vanguard of the polytheists while he was with a group of his companions, and the polytheists said: 'Who are you?' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'We are from water.' They looked at one another and said: 'The tribes of Yemen are many; perhaps they are of them,' and they left."

By his saying (ﷺ) "We are from water," he intended His saying, exalted is He: ﴿created from gushing water﴾ [al-Tariq: 6].

When ʻAbd Allah ibn Rawahah had intercourse with his slave-girl, his wife saw him. She took a knife and came to him, but found him having completed his need.

She said: "If I had seen you where you were, I would have struck it into your neck."

He said: "What did you do?" She said: "If you are truthful, then recite the Qur'an."

He said:

"I testify that the promise of Allah is true, and that the Fire is the abode of the disbelievers.
And that the Throne floats above the water, and above the Throne is the Lord of the worlds.
And carrying it are strong angels, the angels of God, marked."

She said: "I believed in the Book of Allah and denied my own eyes."

This reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he laughed until his molar teeth showed.

Ibn ʻAbd al-Barr said: "This is established from ʻAbd Allah ibn Rawahah."

It is reported from ʻUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "I am amazed at one who knows allusive speech; how does he lie?"

Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, was invited to a meal and said: "I am fasting." Then they saw him eating. They said: "Did you not say, 'I am fasting'?"

He said: "Did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) not say: 'Fasting three days of every month is like fasting the whole year'?"

Muhammad ibn Sirin, when a creditor demanded payment from him and he had nothing with him, would say: "I will give you on one of the two days, God willing." He would be understood to mean that day and the one after it, but he meant the two days of this world and the Hereafter.

(Section)

When you reflect on what Allah, glorified is He, called His servants to contemplate in His Book, it will lead you to knowledge of Him, glorified and exalted is He, and of His oneness, His attributes of perfection, and the descriptions of His majesty: the all-encompassing scope of His power and knowledge, the perfection of His wisdom, His mercy, His beneficence, His kindness, His gentleness, His justice, His pleasure and His anger, His reward and His punishment. Through this He made Himself known to His servants and urged them to reflect upon His signs. We will mention some examples of what Allah, glorified is He, mentioned in His Book, by which one may infer others. Among them is the creation of man, about which He, glorified is He, urged reflection and contemplation in more than one place in His Book, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So let man look at what he was created from.﴾

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And within yourselves; will you not see?﴾

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, indeed We created you from dust, then from a drop, then from a clinging clot, then from a lump of flesh, formed and unformed, that We may make clear to you. And We settle in the wombs whatever We will for a specified term, then We bring you out as a child, then that you may reach your maturity. And among you is one who is taken in death, and among you is one who is returned to the most abject age, so that he knows nothing after having known.﴾

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Does man think he will be left neglected? Was he not a drop of semen emitted? Then he became a clinging clot, and He created and proportioned him, and made of him two mates, the male and the female. Is not He able to bring the dead to life?﴾

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Did We not create you from a worthless fluid, then place it in a secure place for a known term? Then We determined, and how excellent are We as determiners.﴾

And He said: ﴿Does man not see that We created him from a drop, and then he is a clear adversary?﴾

And He said: ﴿And We certainly created man from an extract of clay. Then We placed him as a drop in a secure place. Then We made the drop a clinging clot, then We made the clot a lump, then We made the lump bones, then We clothed the bones with flesh; then We produced him as another creation. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators.﴾

This is frequent in the Qur'an, calling the servant to look and reflect upon the beginning of his creation, its middle, and its end. For his own self and his creation are among the greatest proofs of his Creator and Originator, and nothing is closer to man than himself. In it are wonders that indicate the greatness of Allah, such that lifetimes pass without grasping part of them, while he is heedless of them and turns away from reflecting on them. Had he reflected upon his own self, what he would know of the wonders of its creation would have restrained him from his disbelief. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Woe to man, how ungrateful he is! From what thing did He create him? From a drop He created him and determined him. Then He made the way easy for him. Then He causes him to die and buries him. Then, when He wills, He will raise him up again.﴾

Therefore, the Exalted has not repeated for our ears and minds the mention of this, so that we would hear the words *nutfah* (a drop of semen), *ʿalaqah* (a clinging clot), *mudghah* (a lump of flesh), and *turab* (dust), nor merely to utter them, nor merely to inform us of that. Rather, it is for a matter beyond all of this, which is the purpose of the address, and to which this discourse leads. So consider now the *nutfah* with the eye of insight. It is a drop of despised, weak, filthy water. If an hour passed over it, it would rot and stink. How did the Lord of lords, the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, extract it from between the backbone and the ribs, submissive to His power, obedient to His will, made docile in its movement despite the narrowness of its paths and the variety of its channels, until He drove it to its place of rest and gathering? And how did the Exalted join the male and the female, cast love between them, and by the chain of desire and affection lead them to the union that is the cause of the child's formation and creation? And how did He determine the joining of those two waters, though each is far from the other, driving them from the depths of the veins and organs and gathering them in one place, and giving them a firm settlement that no air can reach to corrupt it, nor cold by His praise, nor any accident that could reach it, nor any blight that could overpower it?

Then He turned that white drop, mixed with color, into a red clot inclining to blackness. Then He made it a lump of flesh, differing from the clot in its color, its reality and its form. Then He made it bones, bare, with no covering upon them, differing from the lump in shape, form, measure, texture and color. And consider how He divided those similar and equal parts into nerves, bones, veins, tendons, the dry and the soft, and what lies between them. Then how He bound some of them to others with the strongest and firmest bond, furthest from dissolution. And how He covered them with flesh, which He set upon them, making it a container, a covering and a guardian for them, and making them bearers of it and sustainers of it, so that the flesh subsists by them and they are preserved by it. And how He shaped them, giving them the best form, and split for them hearing, sight, mouth, nose and all the other openings, extended the two hands and the two feet and spread them out, and divided their extremities with fingers, then divided the fingers into joints. He assembled the inner organs: the heart, the stomach, the liver, the spleen, the lungs, the womb, the bladder and the intestines, each of which has a measure specific to it and a benefit specific to it.

Then consider the perfect wisdom in the structure of the bones as the support and pillar of the body. And how their Lord and Creator determined them with varying measures and varying shapes: some small, some large, some long, some short, some curved, some round, some thin, some broad, some solid, and some hollow. And how He assembled some within others: some whose assembly is like the male within the female, and some whose assembly is only a joining. And how their shapes vary according to the variation of their benefits, like the molars, for since they are the instrument of grinding, they were made broad; and since the teeth are the instrument of cutting, they were made pointed and sharp. And since the human being needs movement with the whole body and with some of its limbs, to move about for his needs, He did not make his bones one bone, but many bones, and placed between them joints so that movement might be easy through them, and the measure and shape of each one were set according to the movement required of it. And how He tightened the joints and limbs and bound some to others with tendons and ligaments, which He grew from one end of the bone and attached one end of the bone to the other end like a band for it. Then He placed on one end of the bone projections extending outward from it, and on the other end hollows sunk into it, matching the shape of those projections, so that they enter into them and fit upon them. So when the servant wishes to move a part of his body, it is not hindered for him. And had there been no joints, that movement would have been impossible for him.

And reflect on the manner of the creation of the head and the great number of bones in it, to the point that it is said they are fifty-five bones of differing shapes, measures and benefits. And how the Exalted set it upon the body and made it high, like the height of a rider over his mount. And since it is high above the body, He placed in it the five senses and all the instruments of perception: hearing, sight, smell, taste and touch. And He placed the organ of sight at its front, so that it would be like a vanguard, a sentinel and a scout for the body. And He constructed each eye of seven layers, each layer having a specific description, a specific measure and a specific benefit, such that if one of those seven layers were lost or moved from its form and place, the eye would be disabled from seeing. Then the Exalted set, within those seven layers, a wondrous creation, which is the pupil of the eye, the size of the lens, by which it sees what is between the east and the west, and the earth and the sky. He made it in the eye as the heart is among the organs: it is its king, and those layers, the eyelids and the lashes are its servants, its screen and its guards. "So blessed be Allah, the best of creators" (23:14).

Consider how the form, shape and measure of the two eyes are beautiful, then how He made the eyelids a covering, a shield, a protection and an adornment for them. Thus they receive from the eye harm, dust and grime, and shield it from the harmful cold and the harmful heat. Then He planted on the edges of those eyelids the lashes, as beauty and adornment, and for other benefits beyond beauty and adornment. Then He deposited in them that seeing light and dazzling radiance which pierces what is between the sky and the earth, and then pierces the sky, reaching beyond the sight of what lies above it, of the stars. The Exalted has deposited this wondrous secret in this small measure, such that the image of the heavens is impressed in it despite the vastness of their expanses and the remoteness of their horizons.

He split for it hearing, and created the ear in the best of its creation and most effective in achieving its purpose. He made it hollow like a seashell, to gather the sound and convey it to the ear canal, and so that it may sense the crawling of an insect within it, and hasten to remove it. He placed in it folds, hollows and windings that hold the entering air and sound, breaking their sharpness, and then conveying them to the ear canal. And one of the wisdoms in this is that the path becomes long for the creature, so it does not reach the ear canal until it awakens or is alerted by its holding. There is also in it other wisdom beside this.

Then the wisdom of the Lord, the Creator, the Exalted, required that He make the water of the ear extremely bitter, so that no creature passes it or cuts through it entering the inner ear; rather, when it reaches it, the ear devises the means for its return. And He made the water of the eyes salty, to preserve them, for they are a delicate fat susceptible to corruption, so the saltiness of their water is for their protection and preservation. And He made the water of the mouth sweet and pleasant, so that by it one perceives the tastes of things as they are. For if it were otherwise, it would transform them to its own nature, just as whoever has bitterness in his mouth finds the tastes of things that are not bitter to be bitter, as it is said:

"And whoever has a bitter mouth, being sick,
finds the pure water bitter to him."

And He, glorified is He, set the bridge of the nose upon the face, so He beautified its form, shape and placement. He opened in it two nostrils and separated them with a partition. He deposited in them the sense of smell (ḥāssat al-shamm) by which one perceives the various kinds of scents, the pleasant and the foul, the beneficial and the harmful, so that one may draw air through it and it may carry the air to the heart, which is refreshed and nourished by it. Then He did not place within it the twists and folds that He placed in the ear, lest it retain the scent, weaken it and cut off its passage. He made it an outlet into which the superfluities of the brain descend and gather, and from which they then exit. His wisdom required that its upper part be narrower than its lower part, because if its lower part were wide, those superfluities would gather in it and exit with ease. Also, it takes in air, fills itself, and then rises a little along its passage until it reaches the heart, arriving without harming or disturbing it. Then He separated the two nostrils with a partition between them, as a wisdom and a mercy from Him. For since it is a conduit and a passage that shields what descends from the head and the breath that rises through it, He placed in its middle a partition so that it would not be corrupted by what flows through it, and so that it would not prevent the inhaling of breath. Rather, either the superfluities descending from one of the two openings generally settle there, leaving the other for breathing, or they flow through both and divide, so the nose is never fully blocked and there remains an entrance for breathing. Furthermore, since it is one organ and one sense, and not two organs and two senses like the two ears and the two eyes, whose plurality wisdom required, it may happen that one of them is afflicted or exposed to a calamity that prevents it from perfect function, while the other remains sound, so the benefit of this sense is not entirely lost. Since the presence of two noses on the face would be a conspicuous thing, He set one nose upon it and placed in it two openings, separated by a partition, which operates in the manner of the plurality of the two eyes and ears in benefit, though it is one. So blessed is Allah, the Lord of the worlds, the best of creators.

He, glorified is He, split the mouth for the servant in the best place and fitted it for him, and deposited in it benefits and the instruments of taste and speech, and the instruments of grinding and cutting, whose wonders dazzle the intellects. He deposited in it the tongue, which is one of His signs that point to Him, and He made it the interpreter of the king of the organs, clarifying and conveying on his behalf. Just as He made the ear a messenger who conveys and delivers to him, so it is his courier that conveys information to him, while the tongue is his courier and messenger who conveys on his behalf what he wants. His wisdom, glorified is He, required that this messenger be protected, guarded and concealed, not exposed or uncovered, like the ear, the eye and the nose. For those organs, since they convey from the outside to him, were made prominent and apparent. But since the tongue conveys from him to the outside, He made for it a protected covering, because there is no benefit in exposing it, since it does not take anything from the outside to the heart. Also, since it is the most noble of the organs after the heart, and its position relative to the heart is that of its interpreter and vizier, He spread over it a canopy that veils and protects it, and placed within that canopy like the heart within the chest. Furthermore, it is among the most delicate and soft of the organs, and the most moist, and it acts only through the moisture surrounding it. Had it been exposed, it would be subject to heat, dryness and desiccation, which would prevent it from acting, along with other wisdoms and benefits.

Then He, glorified is He, adorned the mouth with the teeth it contains, which are its beauty and adornment, and by which the servant's sustenance and nourishment are sustained. He made some of them grinders for crushing and some tools for cutting. He made their roots firm, sharpened their tips, whitened their color, and arranged their rows with equal tips and harmonious order, as if they were pearls strung together in whiteness, clarity and beauty. Glorified is He, He encircled this with two walls and deposited in them benefits and wisdoms, namely the two lips. He made their color, shape, placement and form beautiful, and made them a covering and lid for the mouth. He made them the completion of the articulation points of speech and its final limit, just as He made the farthest part of the throat its beginning, and the tongue and what is adjacent to it its middle. For this reason most of the work of articulation is done by them, since they are the intermediary. His wisdom required that He make the lips pure flesh, without bone or sinew, so that by them one may be able to suck drinks, and so that their opening and closing would be easy for him. He singled out the lower jaw for movement, because moving the lighter part is better, and because it contains the noble organs, so He did not risk them in motion.

Glorified is He, He created the throats of different shapes, in narrowness and breadth, roughness and smoothness, hardness and softness, length and shortness. Thus voices differ enormously, and two voices hardly resemble one another except rarely. For this reason the sound opinion is that the testimony of a blind man is accepted, since he distinguishes between persons by their voices just as the seeing person distinguishes them by their appearances, and the confusion that occurs between voices is like the confusion that occurs between forms.

Glorified is He, He adorned the head with hair and made it a garment for it, because it needs it. He adorned the face with the various shapes and measures of hair that He grew upon it. He adorned it with the eyebrows, made them a shield against what drips from the scalp to the eyes, shaped their arch and beautified their line. He adorned the eyelids with eyelashes. He also adorned the face with the beard, and made it a perfection, dignity and majesty for a man. He adorned the lips with what He grew above them as the mustache and below them as the goatee. Likewise, glorified is He, He created the two hands, which are the servant's instrument, his weapon and the capital of his livelihood. He made their length such that they reach whatever part of his body he wishes, and He made the palm broad so that he may grasp and open. He divided it into five fingers, divided each finger into three phalanges, and the thumb into two. He placed the four fingers on one side and the thumb on the other, so that the thumb can turn to all of them. Thus they came in the best arrangement, suited for grasping, spreading, and handling tasks. Even if the first and the last of mankind were to gather to devise, by the subtlety of their thinking, another arrangement of the fingers besides this one, they would find no way to it. Blessed is He who, had He willed, would have made them otherwise. Had He made them one flat sheet like a plate, the servant could not have accomplished his interests, the various kinds of his dealings, the delicate crafts, writing, and other things. If he spread his fingers they would be a tray upon which he places what he wishes; if he gathered and clenched them they would be a club and an instrument for striking; and if he placed them between closing and spreading they would be a ladle with which he takes and holds what he grasps. He set the nails upon their tips as an adornment, support and protection, and so that he may pick up with them fine things that the finger-flesh cannot reach. He made them a weapon against other animals and birds, an instrument for his livelihood, and so that a person may scratch his body with them when needed. Thus the nail, which is the least and most insignificant of things, if a person lacked it and then an itch appeared, his need for it would become intense, and nothing could take its place in scratching his body. Then He guided the hand to the place of the itch so that it reaches it, even in sleep and heedlessness, without any need to seek. Had he asked someone else, he would not have found the place of the itch except after fatigue and hardship.

Then consider the profound wisdom in making the bones of the lower body thick and strong, because they are its foundation, while the bones of its upper part are less thick and hard, because they are carried.
